Science Bulletin.title: X-ray scattering insights into crystallization, degradation, and heterogeneity of mixed-halide perovskites.
Science Bulletin.abstract: Mixed-halide perovskites have emerged as indispensable light absorbers for high-efficiency tandem photovoltaics, yet their compositional complexity and processing sensitivity demand advanced structural characterization to elucidate film formation, evolution, and degradation across multiple length and time scales. While previous reviews primarily focus on basic tutorials or specific topics like crystallization and degradation, a systematic methodological framework for advanced X-ray platforms remains absent. This review bridges this critical gap by establishing a comprehensive spatiotemporal characterization paradigm. Methodologically, it shifts analysis from static observations to dynamic, nanoscale-resolved, multimodal investigations, enabling mechanistic links among film formation, operational evolution, and heterogeneity-driven segregation. Furthermore, we highlight critical forward-looking perspectives, including the integration of artificial intelligence-assisted automated analysis, upscaled in situ characterization setups, and multimodal characterization. This review aims to equip the community with advanced structural-probing strategies to overcome the bottlenecks of tandem photovoltaics and accelerate their commercialization.

Microbiome.title: A specialized microbiome enriched in nitrification and halogen cycling potential resolved from multi-omics investigation of a Caribbean suboxic and acidic marine sinkhole
Microbiome.abstract: Background The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 Results We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected. Video Abstract

Nucleic Acids Research.title: QPD: a comprehensive database integrating global quarantine regulations with biological, molecular, and spatial resources.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Quarantine pests pose major threats to global biosafety, agriculture, and biodiversity. However, information of their regulatory status, biology, distribution, and molecular resources remains fragmented across multiple sources, which hinders the in-depth analysis of quarantine pests. Here, we present the Quarantine Pest Database (QPD, https://qpests.insect-genome.com), an open-access resource that integrates global regulations with biological knowledge, multi-omics sequences, and distribution of quarantine pests. QPD integrates official quarantine pest lists, complementary phytosanitary notifications, and distribution records of 231 countries and regions, covering 9849 regulated pest taxa, 7666 host plants, 2057 genome assemblies, 4877 transcriptomes, and 1 311 846 DNA barcode sequences. We also provide 21 747 habitat suitability maps for 4350 quarantine pests under historical and future climate conditions. Each pest entry contains the comprehensive information of standardized taxonomy and jurisdiction-specific quarantine status with host associations, distribution records, morphological descriptions, images, literature references, and available omics resources. Moreover, QPD provides interactive browsing and retrieval, DNA barcode finding, global distribution visualization, and model-based habitat suitability maps. To the best of our knowledge, QPD is the first database to integrate global quarantine regulations with biological, molecular, and spatial information of quarantine pests, providing a centralized resource for the community of pest risk assessment and biosecurity research.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Sequence resources of the National Center for Biotechnology Information in 2027.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) provides three principal resources containing DNA, RNA, and protein sequence data: the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), GenBank®, and the Reference Sequence (RefSeq™) collection. All resources are free to the public. SRA and GenBank are part of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration and share data daily. After summarizing the current state of these resources, we review significant updates in the past two years, including these to the Submission Portal, the primary interface for submitting data to SRA and GenBank. We also describe access points for these data including NCBI Datasets' website and programmatic interface, and present improvements in NCBI's main sequence analysis and visualization tools, such as annotation pipelines, BLAST, and the Multiple Comparative Genome Viewer.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: GPCRdb in 2027: new structure and ligand data and analysis tools, and updated data mapper and snakeplot visualizations.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors database (GPCRdb) enables research on GPCRs through tailored resources for reference data, analysis, visualization, experiment design, and dissemination. Our 7th major update to GPCRdb brings extensive updates to the structural and ligand resources, along with several improvements that facilitate easier use. The Structure coverage page has been overhauled to better overview all experimental structures and to break these down into a GPCR class, receptor family, or an individual receptor. We have expanded the annotation on the Structures page by combining AI with manual curation. We add structure models of drug- and peptide-GPCR complexes generated by Boltz-2 and AlphaFold2-Multimer, respectively, and score their confidence. For ligands, we have enhanced the data in the GPCR-ligand interactions resource, implemented variants distinguishing stereoisomers, salts, and labeled versions, assigned persistent identifiers enabling lookup and database cross-linking, and visualized peptide sequences in 2D. Finally, the Data mapper page now has a simplified data input directly in the web interface enabling swift mapping of users' own data for receptors visualized as a GPCRome wheel, tree, clusters, list, or heatmap. Together, these new features aid a multitude of use cases spanning from basic research on GPCR structure-function to drug design. GPCRdb is available at https://gpcrdb.org.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PVDive: the plant virus diversity database.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Plant viruses are a diverse class of infectious agents affecting agricultural crop production, plant health, and international movement of plant material. While availability and accessibility of scientific data related to plant viruses is essential for plant protection activities, scientific research, diagnostics, plant breeding, and beyond, publicly available data on plant viruses are at present not easily accessible; they are non-standardized, scattered across different resources, poorly interlinked, and not easily searchable by scientists or digital agents. We present PVDive (Plant Virus Diversity Database; https://pvdive.dsmz.de), a freely accessible resource providing high-quality, standardized, and integrated data associated with plant viruses. PVDive primarily offers information at the level of individual plant virus isolates and samples originating from the plant virus collection of the Leibniz Institute DSMZ (Germany). The data are integrated with information on plant virus species and host plants available in existing public resources and their access is centralized in a single platform. Through an intuitive, user-friendly interface with a number of search functionalities and a RESTful application programming interface, PVDive improves findability, accessibility, retrievability, and interoperability of plant virus data. To support data exploration, the platform also includes tools such as advanced search, sequence viewer, host gallery, and interactive data views.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PDBe in 2027: integrating literature annotations, molecular dynamics data, and AI-ready access.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe; pdbe.org) provides open access to experimentally determined biomacromolecular structures and enriches these data with biological and functional context. Here, we describe recent developments that expand the information connected to PDB structures and introduce new ways for researchers and computational tools to access it. Literature integration has been extended to additional open-access publications, substantially increasing the availability of residue-level annotations mined from the scientific literature. Cross-links to molecular dynamics simulations in MDposit have been established, and simulation-derived residue-level annotations, including relative solvent accessibility and membrane-related properties, have been integrated into PDBe-KB (pdbekb.org). PDBe entry pages now expose additional experimental and sequence information, links to related resources, and extended PDB identifiers. Protein channel, tunnel, and pore analyses generated using MOLE have also been incorporated into our weekly release pipeline and made available for download. Improved API documentation facilitates the discovery of data fields and search parameters, while three Model Context Protocol servers facilitate agentic access to the PDBe APIs, Search, and the PDBe-KB knowledge graph. Together, these developments make structural data and its wider biological context easier to discover, interpret, and reuse through both conventional and agentic workflows.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CROST 2.0: an expanded repository of spatial transcriptomics.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: CROST (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/crost) is a public spatial transcriptomics resource that offers curated datasets, standardized analytical results, structured spatial knowledge, and interactive exploration tools. In version 2.0, our collection has expanded to 544 projects and 3538 samples, nearly a three-fold increase from version 1.0 (182 projects and 1033 samples). We have also substantially expanded the derived resources for spatial colocalization and spatially variable cancer genes. To facilitate spatial microenvironment analysis, CROST 2.0 introduces an analytical framework comprising niche-associated differential expression, spatially resolved gene-set activity analysis, spatial interaction hotspot and topic analyses, and molecular and cell-type niche analysis. CROST 2.0 also provides the Spatial Compare function to compare spatial gene expression, cell-type distributions, and niche composition across samples. It introduces the Cancer NicheDE module to systematically characterize cancer niche-associated differential expression and integrates an online cell-type annotation tool, SCType, enabling the use of single-cell reference information in spatial transcriptomic analysis. These updates extend CROST into an integrated spatial transcriptomics resource for characterizing spatial microenvironments, investigating cancer-associated spatial features, and comparing spatial patterns across samples.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PubChem 2027 update.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) is a public chemical information resource that serves scientific communities across various domains, as well as the general public. Over the past 2 years, substantial changes have been made to PubChem. The addition of over 100 new data sources has broadened its data coverage. A new data collection, RefChem, containing chemical records compiled by the PubChem team from authoritative and curated sources, was introduced to improve annotation mapping and disambiguation and to provide better access to information on substances with non-discrete structures. The Quick Search supports general exploration across multiple data collections, while the Advanced Search provides more structured, fielded search options for individual collections. The new Search History page enables users to formulate complex queries using Boolean operators. Major updates were also made to the Classification Browser and Co-occurrence Panels. Updates to PubChemRDF improved its search performance and interoperability. Practical guidance was provided for its efficient use in cloud environments. This article provides an overview of the latest updates to PubChem.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: proMGE2-a planetary-scale resource of mobile genetic elements in microbial (meta)genomes.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: proMGE is a resource of prokaryotic mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that systematically catalogues MGEs from prokaryotes, their intercellular spread, antimicrobial resistance gene carriage, and MGE nesting interactions. We present proMGE2 featuring a 6X expansion, a total of >16.4 million MGEs from 670k high-quality isolate genomes, and 180k metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), spanning diverse MGE categories: transposons and insertion sequences, phages, phage-like elements, conjugative elements, mobility islands, and integrons. proMGE2 includes MGEs from MAGs derived from environmental microbiomes, encompassing ~50k samples across several major habitat types. proMGE2 provides a standardized MGE reference collection of >5 million non-redundant MGE sequences drawn from our curated database, and enables identification of MGEs in user-provided genomes. proMGE2 captures MGE diversity and their functional potential at unprecedented scale to support future research of mobile genetic elements and transfer of genetic material in microbes. The database is available at http://promge.embl.de/.

Genome Biology.title: The rise, evolution and future of whole genome projects in Asian populations
Genome Biology.abstract: Asia contains over 60% of the global population and vast genetic diversity, yet its genomic resources remain underrepresented. Over the past decade or so, regional research has evolved from fragmented surveys into large-scale national precision medicine initiatives. Here, we examine how these sequencing efforts collectively form an emerging Asian genomic infrastructure. We discuss future directions to close critical gaps in Central Asia, minority populations, cross-project interoperability, and equitable access, highlighting the transition toward interoperable, clinical-grade genomic ecosystems supporting precision medicine across the continent.

Microbiological Research.title: Interaction between phosphate-solubilizing bacteria and biochar in soil microecological regulation.
Microbiological Research.abstract: The paradox of "high phosphorus reserve but low availability" in soils is a core challenge constraining global agricultural sustainability. Phosphate-solubilizing bacteria (PSB), as a green alternative to chemical phosphate fertilizers, have great application potential. However, their field application has long been limited by three major bottlenecks: poor colonization, low efficiency, and functional instability. This review synthesizes the phosphate solubilization mechanisms of PSB, the construction of synthetic microbial communities, and carrier-mediated microecological regulation strategies. This review highlights the mechanism of carrier-mediated microecological regulation, also identifies gaps in knowledge, and emphasizes the need for further research to elucidate the interfacial interaction mechanisms between PSB and biochar, as well as targeted regulation strategies for the rhizosphere microbial network. Based on this, the carrier-mediated microecological regulation strategy is expected to break through the bottleneck in the field application of PSB, facilitating its transition from the laboratory to the field, and providing important technical support for the efficient utilization of phosphorus resources and the green development of agriculture.

Microbiological Research.title: DksA orchestrates redox-sensitive virulence trade-off between P fimbriae and K1 capsule expression to promote Escherichia coli-induced sepsis.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) is a leading cause of life-threatening sepsis worldwide. A key unresolved question in ExPEC pathogenesis is how these strains initiate and drive severe, high-mortality sepsis. RNA polymerase (RNAP)-binding transcriptional regulator DksA is known to mediate bacterial stress responses. Here, we demonstrate that DksA acts as a critical regulator of ExPEC-induced sepsis. DksA functions as a redox-sensitive molecular switch that modulates virulence trade-off between P fimbriae-mediated adhesion and K1 capsule-dependent immune evasion via the novel sRNA PRs37 (originally designated sRNA037), directly repressing the major pilin subunit PapA. DksA binds RNAP to repress transcription of PRs37 and K1 capsule operons. Oxidative stress triggered by oxidants such as H₂O₂ induces cysteine oxidation of DksA, relieving its transcriptional repression and enhancing ExPEC immune evasion. This DksA redox-dependent regulation operates independently of molecular chaperones and the stringent response. This DksA-orchestrated virulence trade-off serves as a key determinant for the establishment and progression of E. coli sepsis. Our findings deepen the understanding of complex host-pathogen interactions and provide a theoretical foundation for developing novel anti-infective strategies.

Microbiological Research.title: Mechanistic insights into the selective ligninolysis of wheat straw by the grass-litter decomposer Agrocybe pediades: A multi-omics and chemical study.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Agrocybe pediades, a saprotrophic grass-litter-decomposing fungus of the order Agaricales, was studied for its potential to degrade all major components of plant cell walls (PCWs) as inferred from the enzymes encoded in its genome. When grown on wheat straw, this fungus preferentially degraded lignin and hemicelluloses while largely preserving cellulose. To uncover the molecular basis of this selective ligninolysis, we combined genomic, transcriptomic, exoproteomic and metabolomic analyses. Early stages of lignocellulose degradation were characterized by strong mobilization of H2O2-producing enzymes together with ligninolytic class-II peroxidases (PODs). Among ligninolytic PODs, manganese peroxidases were the most abundant. Their ligninolytic activity was related to the potential oxidation of phenolic lignin via Mn³ ⁺ chelates and of non-phenolic lignin through unsaturated lipid peroxidation. Notably, a highly transcribed high-redox-potential lignin peroxidase was also secreted during wheat straw delignification. This oxidative stage was accompanied by sequential transcription and secretion of hemicellulose-active enzymes, suggesting a stepwise xylan degradation. Enzymes targeting other PCW polysaccharides increased during growth. Although most lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases were transcribed, they were not detected in the exoproteome, suggesting that their contribution to cellulose degradation may have been limited. This, together with possible modulation of Fenton chemistry, may have contributed to the limited cellulose degradation observed. Additionally, insights were gained into the intracellular metabolism of sugars and aromatics released during the process. This multi-omics approach, supported by 2D-NMR and chemical analyses, provides valuable insights into selective delignification by A. pediades, contributing to our understanding of selective ligninolysis, an underexplored process with potential for plant biomass valorization.

Microbiological Research.title: Natural polysaccharides targeting gut microbiota in renal fibrosis: Novel molecular mechanisms and therapeutic strategies.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Kidney disease, including acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), represent a major global health burden and are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. AKI is an overwhelming complication of acute disease that leads to the CKD development and ultimately progresses to end-stage renal disease. AKI and CKD are inter-related clinical and pathophysiological disorders. Current treatments, including dialysis and transplantation, are costly and not curative. Natural polysaccharides, widely distributed in medicinal plants and fungi, are important active components with broad healthcare applications. As a natural modulator of gut microbiota (GM), natural polysaccharides play an important role in regulating intestinal inflammation and gut microbial dysbiosis. This review summarizes the pathogenesis and underlying molecular mechanisms of renal fibrosis associated with GM dysbiosis, providing therapeutic strategies and targets for polysaccharide remodeling of the GM to improve kidney disease. We further systematically present the beneficial effects of natural polysaccharides on kidney disease through various molecular mechanisms, such as Toll-like receptor 4, G-protein-coupled receptors, NOD-, LRR- and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 inflammasome, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor, IƙB/NF-ƙB and Keap1/Nrf2 signaling pathways via regulating gut microbial-derived metabolites, such as lipopolysaccharide, short-chain fatty acids, and uremic toxins. These studies expand the understanding of the therapeutic effects and underlying molecular mechanism of natural polysaccharides on kidney disease and expound a clear pathophysiological rationale for the treatment of kidney disease. This review provides targeted therapeutic strategies for kidney disease prevention and management by modulating GM, highlighting the potential of natural polysaccharides as prebiotics in clinical practice.

Water Research.title: Heteroatom-modified sulfidated zero-valent iron: mechanistic insights and perspectives on data-mechanism-driven materials design.
Water Research.abstract: Sulfidated zero-valent iron (S-ZVI) is a promising reductive material for groundwater and soil remediation, yet its application is constrained by toxic H2S release, low-valent sulfur oxidation-induced deactivation, and limited selectivity toward priority pollutants in co-contaminated systems. Co-introducing sulfur with heteroatoms, including carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, boron, and main-group or transition metals, provides a complementary strategy to simultaneously tune mobility, reactivity, selectivity, and durability. This review critically examines the chemical principles and sulfidation pathways governing S-ZVI performance, with emphasis on the design, synthesis, and synergistic mechanisms of sulfur-heteroatom co-modification. We distill general principles linking sulfidation chemistry, geometric/electronic structure, and interfacial reactions, and summarize multiscale characterization and computational approaches for resolving synergistic mechanisms. We then propose a data- and mechanism-driven framework integrating machine learning with quantum chemical calculations for intelligent S-ZVI design, and advocate broader reporting of ineffective or detrimental modifications with mechanistic elucidation to expand unbiased AI training datasets. We also call for shifting S-ZVI research from single-pollutant systems toward realistic co-contamination scenarios, where competitive reactions can guide structural engineering to selectively remove highly toxic or reaction-facilitating pollutants first. Emerging opportunities in multi-strategy coupling and field-scale applications are discussed, aiming to accelerate the transition from empirical trial-and-error toward predictable synthesis and engineering deployment.

Water Research.title: Mechanistic insights into static magnetic field-enhanced removal of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from wastewater by constructed wetlands: Computational simulation and microbial community dynamics.
Water Research.abstract: Microbial degradation is the dominant pathway for pollutant removal in constructed wetlands (CWs). Static magnetic fields (SMFs) were employed as a promising strategy to enhance pollutant removal, as they can effectively promote microbial activity and metabolic capacity without additional chemical amendments. Here, COMSOL-based magnetic-field simulation, plant physiological assays, extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) characterization, and metagenomics were integrated to examine the regulatory effects of SMF intensity and spatial heterogeneity on microbial community structure, functional potential, and benzo[k]fluoranthene (B[k]F) biodegradation. B[k]F removal showed an intensity-dependent threshold response, with 150 mT increasing mean removal efficiency by 14.31% relative to the control. COMSOL simulations showed that 150 mT produced the largest effective SMF zone, covering 39.53% of the reactor volume. This treatment enhanced plant photosynthetic performance, potentially supporting rhizosphere microbial metabolism through plant-derived carbon and oxygen supply and increased EPS concentrations to 30.01 ± 3.19 and 23.59 ± 4.68 mg L⁻¹ in the upper and lower layers, respectively. Metagenomic analysis revealed enrichment of key polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) degrading bacteria affiliated with Actinomycetota (45.20%). At 150 mT, enhanced tricarboxylic acid cycling and oxidative phosphorylation accelerated microbial energy metabolism and promoted conversion of high-molecular-weight B[k]F into low-molecular-weight aromatic acids. These findings suggest that optimized SMFs enhance PAH removal through coordinated plant-microbe responses, thereby providing a basis for designing magnetically intensified CWs as a chemical-free wastewater treatment strategy.

Water Research.title: Isolation of Dehalococcoides mccartyi JC20 and genome-centric metatranscriptomic identification of Aminivibrio sp. as a candidate vitamin B(12) producer.
Water Research.abstract: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for reductive dehalogenases, yet many organohalide-respiring bacteria, including Dehalococcoides mccartyi, are B12-auxotrophic and rely on syntrophic partners for B12 supply. Here, we used genome-centric metatranscriptomics to investigate the B12-cross-feeding network sustaining 1,2-dichloroethane dechlorination in a defined enrichment consortium. Sustained dechlorination proceeded in both B12-free (with other vitamins retained) and completely vitamin‑free treatments at rates of 10.03 ± 0.73 and 9.66 ± 0.05 μM Cl- released·day-1, respectively, with B12 detected at 1.7-3.3 µg∙L-1 after successive transfers. Metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses revealed that Aminivibrio possesses a complete de novo B12 biosynthesis pathway, which was significantly upregulated 123.38-fold under B12-limited conditions, substantially higher than the 7.98-fold upregulation observed in the established B12 producer Acetobacterium. In response to B12 deprivation, D. mccartyi significantly upregulated its B12 transporter operon (btuFCD) and sustained dechlorination via the reductive dehalogenase TceA. Most recovered MAGs were fermentative bacteria that supplied acetate and hydrogen to D. mccartyi. A pure strain of D. mccartyi, designated JC20, was further isolated by dilution-to-extinction and achieved cell densities of 109 cells∙mL-1. Collectively, these findings identify the fermentative Aminivibrio as a previously unrecognized candidate for B12 production and highlight its potential role in supporting Dehalococcoides-mediated dechlorination. This work expands our understanding of the diversity of B12-producing partners in organohalide‑respiring communities and provides insights into the microbial interactions underpinning bioremediation in oligotrophic contaminated environments.

Water Research.title: Adaptive responses and biotransformation of carbamazepine in microalgal-bacterial granular sludge: Microbial succession, functional genes, and toxicity redistribution.
Water Research.abstract: The long-term response and removal mechanisms of microalgal-bacterial granular sludge (MBGS) to persistent pharmaceuticals remain poorly understood. MBGS was exposed to carbamazepine (CBZ) at four concentrations (10 μg L-1, 100 μg L-1, 1 mg L-1, 10 mg L-1) for 35 days. Ammonium and phosphate removal were maintained or enhanced, whereas chemical oxygen demand removal was markedly inhibited at 10 mg L-1. Sludge properties changed non-monotonically without a dose-dependent pattern. CBZ removal was dose-dependent and, in batch tests, adsorption-dominated, with an increasing contribution of biodegradation over time, together with a decrease in the protein fraction and the protein-to-polysaccharide ratio of extracellular polymeric substances. Fifteen transformation products were tentatively identified, formed through epoxidation, hydroxylation, oxidation, ring opening, and rearrangement. Their predicted toxicity was endpoint-dependent, with acridine- and acridone-type products more toxic than CBZ, indicating toxicity redistribution rather than detoxification. The filamentous cyanobacterium Microcoleus increased after operation, particularly at 10 μg L-1, and the heterotrophic genera Sphingomonas, Thauera, and Aquimonas increased in CBZ-exposed reactors, while genes involved in nitrogen metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and energy conversion shifted in composition. Antibiotic resistance genes, mobile genetic elements, and virulence factor genes also shifted in composition, without consistent dose-dependent enrichment. Overall, CBZ removal decreased with increasing loading, whereas COD removal was markedly affected only at 10 mg L-1. Transformation did not necessarily reduce toxicity. These findings show that treatment performance and transformation-product toxicity should be assessed together when applying MBGS to pharmaceutical-contaminated wastewater.

Genome Biology and Evolution.title: Integrated population genomics and phenotypic analyses reveal geographic structure and signatures of recent positive-selection underlying insecticide resistance in Anopheles arabiensis from The Gambia, West Africa.
Genome Biology and Evolution.abstract: Insecticide resistance in malaria vectors is spreading, with newly identified resistance markers raising operational challenges and threatening malaria reduction. Anopheles arabiensis is an important vector in The Gambia; however, the molecular basis of its insecticide resistance remains poorly understood. We observed signals of population structure between coastal and inland An. arabiensis populations in The Gambia, indicating restricted gene flow likely influenced by environmental variation. Pyrethroid and DDT resistance were widespread. However, the prevalence of both phenotypic and genetic insecticide resistance differed between coastal and inland populations. For instance, the Vgsc-L995S and Vgsc-L995F substitutions conferring pyrethroid and DDT resistance were more frequent in coastal populations and were associated with markedly higher phenotypic resistance to these insecticides. We also identified increased frequencies of copy number variation at Cytochrome P450 (Cyp6aa/p, Cyp9k1) and carboxylesterase (Coeae2-7 g) metabolic resistance markers in coastal An. arabiensis. Some observed gene amplifications were unique to Gambian coastal populations, suggesting their independent evolution. Furthermore, we found evidence of genomic regions under recent positive selection on chromosomes 2L:37,282,152-37,298,202 and 3R:28,590,243-28,602,280 with more pronounced selection signals observed among coastal populations. Coastal populations of An. arabiensis displayed an enrichment of resistance alleles, suggesting a localised pressure driving the evolution, selection and spread of resistance mechanisms. These findings underscore the importance of genomic surveillance in concert with bioassays to inform targeted vector control interventions. They also highlight the need to identify the sources and impacts of insecticide pressure acting on recently detected genomic regions under selection in the coastal regions of The Gambia.
